British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Canadian youth climate trial tests federal emissions policy and constitutional duties
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Canada’s first youth-led federal climate trial opened Oct. 26 in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue the federal Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and the 2030 plan fail to cut emissions enough to protect their health and safety. The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Supreme Court agrees to review Trudeau government’s Emergencies Act use
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada agreed on Oct. 22 to hear the federal government’s appeal over its 2022 use of the Emergencies Act during protests in Ottawa and at key border crossings. Two lower courts found the invocation unjustified and ruled that it infringed Charter rights. The Supreme Court will also hear cross-appeals on issues raised by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Canadian Constitution Foundation. The government argues that the lower courts judged its decision with hindsight instead of asking whether officials acted reasonably on the information available at the time. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association says Ottawa is trying to relitigate arguments the courts already rejected. A public inquiry reached a different conclusion from the courts, finding in early 2023 that the government met the high legal threshold, though its commissioner said the factual basis was not overwhelming. No hearing date has been set; a hearing is unlikely before spring 2027 and could take place in the fall.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Carney says Indian Act review may stop short of abolition
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that a federal review of the 1876 Indian Act may not lead to its abolition. The law governs First Nations legal status, reserve lands and aspects of community governance. He said Ottawa will work with First Nations and provincial and territorial governments to consider reforms or possible replacements, with no predetermined outcome. The clarification follows Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s call to abolish the act at a meeting of First Nations leaders and premiers in Ottawa. Carney said the process must be co-developed with First Nations. Some leaders and community members welcomed the discussion, while others warned that change without Indigenous leadership could threaten rights or repeat past paternalism.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Alberta voters rejected starting the legal process for a binding separation referendum, with about 75% choosing to remain in Canada and 25% backing the process in the Oct. 19 vote, according to the complete but unofficial count. Elections Alberta expects to release official results on Oct. 29. Voters supported proposals on immigration and citizenship rules but rejected all four proposed constitutional changes. Premier Danielle Smith has said she will pursue the measures that passed and work with Prime Minister Mark Carney on immigration. Separately, the Alberta government is continuing its appeal of a ruling that quashed a citizen-led separation petition. First Nations chiefs and Alberta’s opposition are urging it to withdraw the appeal; the government says the court decision contained errors of law.

British Columbia voters are choosing a 93-member legislature Saturday in a snap provincial election called two years early, with the governing New Democratic Party (NDP) and the Conservative Party of B.C. running close in final polls. Eby initially cited U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade threat as a reason to seek a new mandate, then said he should have explained more clearly that the legislature had stalled under the NDP’s narrow majority. Eby also accused interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson of serving as a “Trojan horse” for extremists in his party; Doerkson called that characterization “absurd”. Election officials will count election-day ballots by hand because the snap vote left Elections BC too little time to prepare enough tabulators. Officials will electronically tabulate advance-voting and electoral-office ballots and report those results first. Absentee and mail-in ballots will not be included in election-night totals; they are scheduled for the final count from Nov. 6 to Nov. 10.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.

items.title: [downes.ca] The ethical application of AI in learning analytics
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

JISC, Oct 28, 2026

This document follows Jisc's updated learning analytics code of practice to add more on "the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance student engagement monitoring and support organisations to identify learners who may benefit from additional support." I think we should understand that the document refers to 'ethical' in the legal sense rather than the moral sense. That said, it contains a number of common-sense statements about AI in learning analytics, for example, "Where AI tools are provided by third parties, organisations remain responsible for how student data is used" and "'Understanding' a model means being confident in its behaviour through validation and monitoring, not necessarily being able to read its internal workings."
